The cocciopesto floor dotted with white tesserae, with a carpet or threshold with scales, always outlined in white tesserae, must have belonged to the room (31) before its transformation into an apse room; now it is part of a room with an entrance from number 37, equipped with an arched masonry counter, defined by Fiorelli (Fiorelli D, p. 222): "dark passage with hearth equipped with steps".

121. Exedra (31): very deteriorated remains of decoration in the fourth style at the eastern end of the N wall; low plinth with marble cladding (probably Lunense marble) of which some original slabs are preserved. Lower red area, with aedicules alternating with oblong shots. The former contain human figures (see fig. 133), the others borders with palmettes and garlands. The middle area was originally black, with large fields framed by ornamental borders of intricate design. Only the right side field has been partially preserved, occupied in the central part by a painting with a mythological subject executed separately (see figs. 123, 124).
122. Exedra (31), detail of the N face of the pillar between the N wall and the apse: candelabrum painted in yellow, blue, red and white on a black background, now completely faded (see fig. 126).
123. Exedra (31): painting with a mythological subject on the N wall (state of conservation in 1979; see figs. 121, 124). 79 N53835

124. Exedra (31): mythological picture of the N wall (drawing by N.La Volpe; see previous fig.). A photograph by Curtius-Faraglia from the 1920s (DAIR 56.1187) confirms the correctness of La Volpe's etching with regard to the subject of the painting, while the stylistic rendering is less accurate. In 1868, Helbig (H, 288, no.

125. Exedra (31): remains of decoration in the fourth style on wall E (state of conservation in 1979; see fig. below). Above a low plinth clad in Lunense marble, the lower area is divided into three red compartments by a pair of yellow fields, each imitating a panel with gorgoneîon within a central recess. Each of the red side fields shows a panther flying towards the center below a yellow garland hanging from a small central panel containing a pair of dolphins (fig. 127). In the center of the central field is a green panel with an upper tympanum termination, containing a pair of seahorses galloping to the left (see fig.

126. Exedra (31), wall E, decoration in the fourth style (drawing by A. Ala of 1856; see previous fig.). On the basis of a comparison with the remains still in situ and with the photographs of T. Warscher of the thirties, Ala's reproduction can be considered decidedly accurate and faithful. It is based on pencil traces, now preserved in the National Museum of Naples (ADS 613-5, 632-4, 636, 647, 663; cf. Disegnatori, pp. 539, fig. 63; 537, fig. 50; 203, fig. 87; 883, fig. 4; 538, fig. 52; 884, fig. 6) of all the main elements including the two mythological panels.
127. Exedra (31), wall E, detail of the right side field of the lower area (see figs. 125-6): panther in flight below a garland and a small pinax containing two dolphins.
128. Exedra (31), wall E, detail (see figs. 125-6): pair of seahorses galloping in the centre of the lower area.
129. Exedra (31), wall E, detail (cf. figs. 125-6): upper part, very faded, of filigree border between architecture in perspective, to the left of the painting with Leda. 79 N53839

130. Exedra (31), wall E, painting with Leda (60 x 81 cm; see fig. 125): frightened, Leda jumps to her feet, dropping the woollen basket to the right and looking upwards. She is portrayed in a frontal pose, with her mantle floating behind her, one end of which she raises with her right hand, in an attempt to protect the white swan that she holds firmly against her side with her left. Part of the mantle is still resting on the chair together with some cushions and a piece of fabric that covers the back of the chair. Under the chair is a small suppedaneum. In the background you can see a door on the right, the upper part of which seems open.

131. Exedra (31), wall E, painting with sacrificial scene (62 x 80 cm; cf. fig. 126): in the centre is a majestic female figure, standing in an almost frontal pose, with her head turned slightly to the right. On the chiton she wears a cloak that covers her head and characterizes her as a priestess. His left arm is bent, in his left hand he has an unidentified object; the right is resting on the drapery of the cloak below the chest. To its left is a round table on which rests a plate containing some objects, probably fruits. From the left, a girl is approaching, depicted in profile on the right; He has the so-called melon hairstyle and wears a folded peplum above his belt. She seems attracted by a plate or tray that she herself holds in her left hand, while arranging, or balancing, its contents. In the background are trees and a pillar behind the priestess. 79 N53837

132. Exedra (31), S wall, remains of IV style decoration: same scheme as on wall N (see fig. 121), however none of the mythological paintings are preserved. That of the left side field was still in situ in 1863 when it was described by Helbig (H, 321, no. 1392): "On either side of an altar is a standing male figure with red chlamys and with his sword uncovered in his right; in his left hand he holds an object that has now completely disappeared. No heads are preserved of both figures. Below, on a staircase in front of the tent of a temple, the lower part of a figure with green boots and an ankle-length red chiton is visible."
133. Exedra (31), S wall, detail (see fig. 132): female figure inside an aedicule-shaped structure in the lower area.

134. Apotheca (32), seen from the W: white mortar floor with small fragments of brick. The walls are plastered, but probably never received a painted decoration. Numerous holes and iron nails suggest that the room, originally a cubicle, was transformed into a warehouse after 62 AD. 79 N55144

135. Oecus (33): black and white floor mosaic, after 62 AD; white main field enclosed by a large black perimeter band and two narrow black bands. The square emblem in the centre of the room measures 1.15 x 1.15 m (see fig. 136).

136. Oecus (33), black and white floor mosaic, detail: central emblem, with a rosette motif formed by intersecting black and white circles, surrounded by two hexagons intertwined within a circle. The latter is inserted in a square with a calyx between tendrils in each of the four corners. The outer frame is composed of a dog motif running between black bands.

137. Oecus (33), N wall with very deteriorated remains of decoration in the fourth style: black plinth divided into three oblong fields by two vertical cornices; each field preserves traces of ornamental bands, floral motifs, tendrils and garlands. Red middle area with a large aedicule framing a central mythological painting depicting Theseus abandoning Ariadne on the island of Naxos, currently in Naples (see fig. below). Narrow fields with arINS elements. 4, 31.51

138. Oecus (33): mythological painting in the centre of the N wall, (Naples National Museum, inv. 9052; see previous fig.). We have Helbig's description of the painting (H, 255, no. 1217): "Theseus lingers with his left foot on the pier of his boat and looks at Ariadne lying asleep on the shore on bristly blankets. He raises his left hand as if for a monologue, while with his right he stops the reddish cloak lined with blue that covers his

139. Oecus(33), wall E with very deteriorated remains of decoration in the IV style: the scheme is similar to that of the N wall (see fig. 137), however the central mythological painting (height 60 cm, width 51 cm) has never been detached and is now completely faded. It was already partially destroyed in 1868, the year of Helbig's following description (H, 58, no. 215): "Apollo, with a crown, sandals on his feet, iridescent red and violet chlamys on his thighs, sits on a stone, on which a kithara is placed, his left hand pointed to the ground, his right resting on his thigh, looks at a girl who sits in front of him,  with her legs covered " by an iridescent green and light purple robe. This figure, probably Daphne, is almost completely destroyed." 79 N53872

140. Oecus(33), S wall with very deteriorated remains of decoration in the IV style: scheme similar to that of the N and E walls (see figs. 137, 139). Faint traces of a group of floating figures in the centre of the right lateral field, probably the group of Eros and Psyche documented by Horatius Angelini (see fig. below).

141. Oecus (33): floating group in a drawing by H. Angelini, which is said to come from this room, probably from the central part of the right lateral field of the S wall; on the left, Eros with a small cloak floating behind his back, and with a large lyra behind his left shoulder; on the right, Psyche flying towards

142. Vestibule (35): N-W corner with door leading into the northern peristyle on the right, entrance to the cubicle (36) on the left. Instead of three zones, the plaster is applied here in two zones, with the seam line visible 2.05 m from the floor level. Entirely white, with wide red vertical bands (now very faded) along the edges of each wall. In the corner, at a height of 3.70 m, a small part of the ceiling is preserved, also with a white background with a red frame.

143. Vestibule (35), S-W corner: on the right, opening to the northern peristyle, on the left, entrance to the cubicle (36), plaster applied in two days (joint line 2.15 m above the floor level) and painted white. Walls framed by large red bands.
144. Cubicle (36): white lime mortar floor with tiny black volcanic inclusions; fragments of white limestone and bricks are inserted into this base, at almost regular intervals.

145. Cubicle (36), wall O, with remains of decoration in the fourth style (state of conservation in 1979; see fig. below): painting on a white background with a bipartite scheme; in the plinth there is a rectangular central field with an arched top, containing a flowering plant; both side fields are divided by a horizontal border with palmettes; A floral pattern occupies the central part of the upper half. The middle area has a narrow rectangular field in the center with a tall candelabrum with garlands hanging from its top. The edges of the two side fields consist of red lines enclosing a green garland, with a small blue square in each corner and a volute acrotery at the upper corners. In the center of each field is a griffin facing the center of the wall. In the center of the upper area, within an aedicule crowned with a floral motif, is a deer lying to the right, under a garland hanging from the top of two slender candelabra. Each of the fields is flanked by two elegant candelabra with two branches emerging from the flowery top of the main stem, with a wreath knotted in three places, hanging in front of the projecting cornice of the central aedicule and the cornice of the wall, and tied by ribbons at both ends. A pair of cornucopias hang from the garland, to which they are attached with ribbons. Above each candelabrum a band frames a large flower between leaves; a pair of thin diagonal lines decorated with stylized palmettes on both sides.

146. Cubicle (36), wall O, decoration in the fourth style, in a drawing by J.W. Wild (181492) executed around the middle of the nineteenth century (watercolour preserved in the Victoria & Albert Museum, London; inv. no. E. 3983-1938). The remains still visible in situ show that of the many watercolorists who reproduced this painting in the last century, Wild is to be considered the most accurate and reliable. London, Vict. & Albert Museum (Fot. Museum)

147a-b. Cubicle (36), N wall with remains of decoration in the fourth style (state of conservation of 1979; see fig. below). The decorative and chromatic scheme, as well as most of the details, are reflected in the W wall (see figs. 145, 146). Among the secondary differences are the candelabra in the middle area with a twisted stem and a less elaborate top than in the O wall; the globe it supports has no "wings" and the garland has no central node. The main differences can be seen in the upper area, where in the central aedicule, instead of a deer, there seems to be a panther. Part of the aedicule is obliterated by an arched window (framed by a red band) that reaches the lunette. Each of the side fields encloses a pinax containing a bucranium between floral motifs in the lower half, while the upper half is divided by a large vertical ornamental border, on the top of which rests a blue band framing a large rosette with leaves. Each of the lower fields contains a bird (dove?) below an arched garland. The lunette, framed by wide red bands, represents a pond with at least six ducks, some of which flap their wings, and numerous large aquatic plants. A few blue patches indicate water.

148. Cubicle (36), N wall, decoration in the fourth style in a drawing by ].W. Wild (see figs. 147a, 147b). The watercolor reproduces approximately two-thirds of the wall, starting from about half the height of the middle area, and does not include a large part of the right area, which can be reconstructed in a mirror based on the left side.
149. Oecus (39): remains of signino floor in the S-W corner; Fragments of bricks and pieces of yellow tuff and grey limestone are inserted into a white lime base. Probably I century B.C.

150. Oecus (39), N wall with window overlooking the northern peristyle and remains of a very simple decoration in the fourth style. Yellow plinth, bordered at the top by a large red band, without subdivisions and emblem. White middle area, crowned by a molded stucco molding, with palmettes alternating with lotus flowers. The same moulding frames the bezel (see fig. below). No traces of color are preserved.
151. Oecus (39), N-E angle: detail of the E pendentive of the lunette. Stucco moldings with a molded frieze of palmettes alternating with lotus flowers.

152. Oecus(39), S wall with remains of simple decoration in the fourth style (see fig. 150): red band above a yellow plinth; white middle area. At the eastern end of the wall there is a small piece of plaster with a left pendentive of the lunette.

153. Lararium (41), floor at the W end of the room: pieces of marble of irregular shape (pavonazzetto, antique yellow), with a diameter of up to 25 cm, randomly arranged in a base of yellowish lime. Probably late first century BC or early first century AD.

154. Lararium (41), seen from E (state of conservation until 23 November 1980, when the lararium was seriously damaged by the earthquake): entirely white except for the niche, which is about 20 cm deep; the ceiling of the niche is red, the section of wall below it yellow, while in the 15 cm high band above the niche, and framed by protruding moldings, are green, red and yellow bands imitating marble. The back wall of the niche is bordered at the top by a cyma reversa stucco molding, with a frieze of palmettes and molded lotuses (not painted). A similar moulding, but of better workmanship, marks the upper edge of its background, in which an ovolo is added to the frieze with palmettes and lotuses. It was originally painted red, but it seems to have deteriorated considerably already in antiquity and was crudely repaired at some time (perhaps after 62 AD). A third molding decorates the face of the shelf below the niche. The niche is set on the top of a brick arch, the bottom and the left (southern) side of which are painted white, with yellow and red dots and spots imitating marble.

155. Room (44), part S: pink plaster up to a height of 1.50 m from floor level; grey plaster in the upper area, separated by a band about 20 cm high with shears to ensure the adhesion of the strip of plaster intended to cover the joint. It has no painted decoration.
156. Apotheca (52), part S: remains of pale pink plaster on all walls, unpainted. Beam holes for shelves.
157. Cubicle (53), corner S-E: recess for a small bed or bench, with remains of unpainted plaster.
158. Cubicle (54), wall E with recess for the bed (?): remains of unpainted pale pink plaster.

159. Cubicle (55): fairly well preserved floor except in a large area in the central part of the room; fragments of bricks and pieces of white marble and yellow tuff of various shapes and sizes inserted in a base of white lime mortar. Probably I century A.D.

160. Cubicle (55), N wall, seen from S-W: remains of decoration in the first and fourth styles. Red plinth without subdivisions and frames. Yellow middle zone with wide red bands at the edges, divided into two fields by a central band, also probably red. At a height of about 2.50 m from floor level, this simple fourth-style decoration borders on the remains of an older first-style decoration, consisting of a projecting band 15.5 cm high, adorned with a row of squares engraved and outlined in red, in imitation of block masonry (see fig. 161). Above the band, a smooth moulding serves as the base of the bezel, the curve of which is composed of a green band bordered by a cable moulding and a groove painted in red.
161. Cubicle (55), N wall, detail: remains of decoration in the first style with imitation of block masonry; at the bottom, simple decoration in the fourth style (see fig. 160).

162. Cubicle (55), S wall: remains of decoration in the fourth style (red plinth, yellow middle area) bordering on a band in the first style and projecting stucco moulding, at a height of 2.50 m from the floor level (only a small part of it is preserved in the N-E corner; see figs. 160, 161). 79 N55154
163. Cubicle (55), wall E: remains of decoration in the fourth style, similar to that of wall N (see fig. 160), but with a middle area divided into three fields, instead of two.
164. Exedra (56): the white floor mosaic has been preserved along the E wall.
165. Exedra (56), seen from the W, with plastered, but unpainted walls.
166. Kitchen (57): floor in the S part made of large bricks. In the foreground, the mouth of a cistern; in the background, the latrine.

167. Room (58): staircase leading to the upper floor, with unpainted plaster on the O wall. The block of lava with the (modern?) indication of a human face placed on the fifth step of the staircase was brought in recent times and does not belong to the house.

168. Cellar (59): square panel with a white background on wall E with a representation of a snake. The animal wraps itself around various plants, approaching a small crack in the wall, in which a wooden offering tray was probably inserted. At the top of the panel, a garland hangs from the center to both corners, to which it is attached with blue ribbons. Later than 62 A.D. 79 N53859
1. Façade in opus incerta with restoration work in opus listata and in opus brick; on the left is number 41 communicating with the upper floor by a staircase.

2. The wall E with the entrance door, which was also the only source of light in the narrow room, preserves the traces of the roof vault in the course of the holes for the beams which, not having to bear any weight above, were rather thin. The door had four folding leaves, as evidenced by the presence of the holes for the bolts in the lava threshold. The plaster had a white background.

3. The masonry bed was leaning against the W wall with an irregular course due to the protrusion of the S-E corner of the portico of the nearby Casa della Caccia antica. On the walls there are remains of plaster with a white background with red stripes. 79 N62524

2. The large entrances defined by the pillars in opus quadrata di tuff were not restricted by restoration work following the earthquake of 62 and preserved the appearance of a Samnite construction at the front of the workshop until the last years of the city's life.

1. The presence of the staircase in the small hallway at no. 44 is still recognizable by the base made up of blocks of lava on which the wooden part rested; in the N wall you can recognize a terracotta pipe descending from the first floor. 79 N62528

3. On the W wall of the back shop (2) there were traces of the fourth style decoration with the red plinth crossed by yellow squares; the middle area with a white background was divided into panels bordered in red and with carpet edges with two parallel lines, separated by a narrow compartment with a golden candelabrum. 79 N62518

4. The room (3), open on Via della Fortuna with number 47, was intercommunicating with the workshop nos. 45-46 through a lowered arch passage in wall E, in which a terracotta pipe was also inserted for the drainage of the water on the first floor. Traces of rough plaster remain on the walls. 79 N62517

1. View of the façade on Via della Fortuna, with the limestone sidewalk in front and the entrances of the shops at numbers nos. 46-49. Jabs in carefully cut blocks of Nocerino tuff. Walls of the vestibule (1) of house no. 48 in opus încertum. Wall E of the workshop at number 49 with remains of plaster and a semicircular niche (39 x 48 cm, depth 20 cm). Above the niche, a series of rectangular holes for beams.

2. Vestibule (1), wall E, with remains of decoration in the IV style. Black plinth (?) with ornamental motifs. Dark red central area with architectural motifs and female figure in flight. Southern jambs decorated with fake pillars colored in dark red. Opus signinum floor.

3. Atrium (2), section W of the N wall with entrance jamb (1) in blocks of Sarno limestone and walled door communicating with the shop at number 49. Decoration in the fourth style: dark red plinth with swans, sphinxes and plant motifs. Middle area with red and yellow fields with figures in flight of the Season: Autumn with wreath and basket of fruits on a red field to the W.

4. Atrium (2), view of the N area towards the vestibule (1). Impluvium with marble cladding and cocciopesto edges. Two lava cistern mouths, the northern one with a circular lid, the southern one with a limestone puteale. On the N wall of the atrium, decoration in the fourth style with a dark red plinth in which about 70 coin impressions have been preserved.

5. Room (4), view to the W. Small room with vaulted ceiling. Decoration in the fourth style: dark red plinth with ornamental elements in white and yellow (garlands, crowns, dolphins and plant motifs). In the middle and upper areas, architectures painted on a white background of summary execution. Wall O: Torn middle panel; cupids floating in the side fields and Vittoria with crown in the upper area. N wall: medallion with Mercury, in the side panel of the middle area.

6. Room (4), wall O: central panel with representation of Danae and the golden rain (Naples, Museo Naz., inv. no. 9549). Danae wears a yellow cloak and looks over her left shoulder at a cupid who rains golden rain from an amphora. Danae collects the rain in a fold of the cloak that she holds in her left hand. A brown lightning bolt to the left of the panel symbolizes Zeus.

8. Room (4), E side of the S wall, middle area with a white background: in the central panel, Leda with the swan. At the E end of the wall: round with bearded Jupiter, green tunic, sceptre resting on the left shoulder. Architectural details mainly in green, red and pink.

7. Room (4), wall E with a view of the atrium (2) and the rooms to the E of the atrium. N wall: medallion with Selene. S wall: medallion with Jupiter. Red hoof motifs: crowns, griffon vultures and dolphins, bucraniums, plant motifs.

9. Room (4), S wall: detail of the central panel with Leda and the swan. Leda lifts her dark red cloak with her left hand and grabs a goose-like swan with her right. In front of Leda's right foot are the yellow scepter and the lightning bolt of Zeus.
10. Room (4), wall S, side panel O, detail: medallion with Selene with yellow and red chiton and yellow lunar crescent applied to the forehead. On his right shoulder he wears a whip.

11. Room (4), section O of wall N; middle area with central panel depicting Venus Fisher and medallion with Mercury. Upper area with a central aedicule decorated with grotesques, in which there is a female figure draped with patera and garland. The figure rests on a pinax with a representation of a landscape. Rectangular panel in the upper side field with metal vase hanging from a ribbon.
12. Room (4), N wall: detail of the central panel with Venus Fishermix. Venus, draped in a robe that leaves her upper body uncovered, with a crown, sits on a bench and

13. Room (4), wall N, side panel O, detail: medallion with Mercury (diameter about 37 cm) painted in shades of brown and yellow. It has a yellow, winged petasus on its head and holds a light brown caduceus. The medallion is framed by a red border.
14. Room (4), N wall, side panel E, detail: medallion with the Sun, with radiated crown and brown drapery. On his right shoulder rests a whip.

15. Room (6), wall O: scenae frons with yellow architecture and white backgrounds. In the foreground, traces of figures, in brown, part of a depiction of Achilles in Sciros. Dark red plinth with central portico supported by caryatids and winged Erote in the central aedicule. Lime floor with white and colored marble inserts. '79 N60356

16. Room (6), wall W, upper area, detail: central aedicule with a large figure of Mercury seated on a throne, with a dark red and blue cloak, petasus and winged sandals and with a brown caduceus in his right hand. Under this figure, through a fake opening, we can see the glimpse of a tèémenos (?) closed on three sides. 79 N 60371

17. Room (6), W wall, plinth, detail: N caryatid of the central portico with a patera in the right hand. Of the side field on the N side, a floral ornament with scrolls, a band of stylized rosettes and an arched garland are partially visible.

18. Room (6), W wall, N end of the plinth, detail: large yellow, white and green floral ornament in the upper half of the plinth; edge of stylized rosettes. The plinth is defined at the top by a row of dentils.

19. Room (6), wall E: scenae frons of the middle area with a predominance of yellow; openings with a white background; figures in the foreground no longer visible. Dark red plinth with portico supported by caryatids; in the center of the portico, a shrine with a young male figure.
21. Room (6), N wall, middle area, N section, detail: architectural openings in the scenae frons. Brown garland hanging from a central disc.

20. Room (6), S wall, plinth, detail: figure of a young man in the central aedicule, naked except for a cloak that falls from his right shoulder to his back; he rests his right elbow on a plinth and holds a pedum (?). 79 N60359

22. Room (11), N wall with view of the vestibule (1) through the atrium (2), with the N-W corner of the impluvium. Jamb E in opus mixtum, jamb O in Sarno limestone, marble threshold, wall decoration N with alternating red and yellow panels, very deteriorated. Black plinth with ivy omphalòs within a red panel.

23. Room (10), view towards the S with the E section of the peristyle (12) and (13) in the background. Mosaic floor with a prevalence of white tiles, black tile border and central black and white checkerboard motif. Wall paintings E, Se O with marble imitation plinth, predellas with cupids hunters and Nilotic landscapes in the center; Blue middle area with architectural openings on a white background.

24. Room (10), wall E: imitation marble plinth; side predellas with cupids hunters, central predella with Nilotic scene; blue central curtain and white architectural openings on the sides; White top area with fantastic patterns. Central panel removed (see fig. 26).

25. Room (10), wall E, upper part: central blue middle area with hanging drapes containing fruit. Upper area with a young winged male figure in the center, inside a pergola covered with vines. On both sides of the pergola, garlands supporting peacocks and hanging masks. Below, charioteers driving chariots, all framed between the acrotery of the aedicule enclosing the central field of the middle area.

26. Room (10), wall E, central panel (Naples, Museo Naz., inv. no. 9048): Theseus and Ariadne outside the Labyrinth; Ariadne, with a green chiton, hands the skein of thread to Theseus, naked except for a cloak resting on his shoulders and with a sword.
27. Room (10), wall E, central predella and plinth in imitation marble: in the predella a Nilotic scene with pygmies watching over exotic animals.

28. Room (10), wall E, side panel N, detail: figure in flight of a winged Lucifer with a short red cloak and yellow torch. On her wings sits Venus, with a yellow cloak that inflates like a sail behind her shoulders.
29. Room (10), wall E, middle area; side panel S, detail: figure in flight of Winged Victory with chiton and trophy.

30. Room (10), wall O: imitation marble plinth, predellas with cupids hunters on the sides and central Nilotic scene; blue curtain in the central part of the middle area with white side architectural backgrounds; White top area with fantastic patterns. The central panel was torn and half of the central predella was lost.

31. Room (10), wall W, central painting, with Daedalus and Pasiphae (Naples, Museo Naz., inv. no. 8979). Pasiphae wears a purple chiton and sits on a throne. Daedalus has a short blue tunic, holds an axe in his hand and points to a cow on the bottom on wooden wheels.
33. Room (10), O wall, N side panel, detail: figure in flight of Vespers with short purple chiton and high leather boots. On his wings sits Diana-Luna with a lit torch.
32. Room (10), wall O, detail of the side panel S: figure of winged Victory in flight with a red tunic down to her feet holding a crown (?).

35. Room (10), S wall, section E, with part E of the garden (13) in the background. Imitation marble plinth; predella with a hunting scene for cupids; blue middle area; White upper area with fantastic ornamental motifs. In the middle area, winged cupid with a hare and a box. In the upper area, cupid with thyrsus and bunch of grapes, and two lions.

34. Room (10), S wall, W section, with E colonnade of the ambulatory (12) in the background. Imitation marble plinth; predella with hunting scene; blue middle area; White upper area with fantastic ornamental motifs. In the middle area winged cupid with fishing rod (?). In the upper area cupid with thyrsus and bunch of grapes, and lion.

4. Atrium (7), N wall: in the Tuscan atrium with rooms on one side only, in the N section of the W wall are the remains of the staircase that led to the upper floor. AE of the fauces there are two niches of the lararium, of which Avellino (cited in the bibl.) has left an exhaustive description: «But in the wall g there was a shrine or lararium, whatever it may be called, of singular shape. On a red plinth, at the height of five palms of the ground, there was a small frame worked with painted stucco, and submerged in a white stripe were the fragments of a now lost painting representing a person sacrificing near an altar. Above this painting is another small frame of colored stucco on which a base protruded, and on this rested three fluted columns of stucco standing out on the wall, and even now lost, of which only the lower half was with the bases already preserved, with intermediate niches, one of which was certainly rectangular and tinged with red in the interior; the other white inside was restored to a semi-elliptical arch. Another similar half column could be seen at a greater distance to the left near the corner of the wall, nor is it doubtful that there must have been a similar one on the right that closes this kind of aedicule on that side».

6. The E wall of the atrium (7), with the doors of the rooms (8), (9) and (10), was built when the house incorporated these rooms, originally belonging, like (13) and (14), to the House of the Colored Capitals, probably in the middle of the first century AD.

7. The tuff impluvium, 1.27 m wide and 1.40 m long, was classified by Fadda (Fadda, p. 165) in its group 3A. It has a border about 0.47 m wide, also in tuff, and shows two holes for water drainage, on the N and S sides. The puteal visible in fig. 6 evidently does not belong to the furnishings of the house (cf. Avellino 1843: «but devoid of the usual puteale»).

8. Room (8), N wall: it seems that this wall was rebuilt after 62 AD and about 8 cm further S than its original position. The deteriorated IV style decoration is a copy of the lower quality of the paintings on the $ and E walls and the S section of the W wall. In the centre, at a height of about 0.90 m from the floor level, there is a window (height 0.85 m, width 0.75) walled up after the excavation, but which in ancient times connected the room with the workshop at number 55.

9. Room (8), S-W corner. The arch above the door, towards the atrium, was restored after excavation with new bricks and reused tiles. The decorative scheme can be reconstructed thanks to the remains preserved in various points on the walls of the room. The hoof was black and divided into alternately narrow and wide fields. Inside the former were rosettes painted in yellow, light red and green, in the wide fields were green bushes of leaves. The middle area was red, divided, with perforated borders, into fields separated from each other by probably black pilasters. On wall E, in the field on the left, the outlines of a rectangular pinax, 0.24 m high and 0.43 m wide, with the depiction of a bird nibbling on fruit are visible. Avellino (Avellino 1843) mentions a decoration with "various rabesques, vases, needles, fruits and other ornaments", but, apart from the aforementioned pinax, nothing has been preserved of it. In the upper area, the pictorial layer has been completely lost. DAIB 90.2.334 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

21. The furnishings of the viridarium (15) include a three-compartment basin with a marble edge. The three reservoirs communicate through circular holes placed in the separation walls. In the central basin there is a small part of a marble lotus flower (see fig. 26) from which, through a lead pipe, water gushed out.

22. The S walls of the viridarium (15) were decorated with garden paintings. On the S wall there is a mosaic fountain made of polychrome tiles, mainly blue, delicate glass plates and three types of shells. Elegant ornamental motifs embellish the niche of the fountain and its front, on which a Nilotic landscape is depicted in the rectangular painting of the predella. The double-pitched roof retains parts of the original cladding in lead sheets. In the niche was placed a marble statuette of Silenus (see fig. 27). The latter holds in his hand a wineskin from which the water flowed which, flowing on the four steps of the ladder covered with marble, poured into the basin. At the time of the excavation, on the two wings of the ladder and on the edge of the basin were still the reproductions. 4, 56

25. The side walls of the fountain have a completely different type of decoration. On a background made up of small fragments of limestone are inserted large shells and pieces of glass. The surviving glass fragments reveal a great variety of colors, green, blue, turquoise, red, black, white. Some are in solid colors, but most of them were made with the millefiori technique. A6186a) testifies to the state of conservation of the time. Copenhagen, Kunstakad. (Photos. Museum)

2. Façade, W section. This part of the façade rests directly on the tuff corner of the adjacent Casa della Parete nera (VII 4, 59). Between this and the limestone orthostats of the entrance, the wall is in opus incertum of lava. The closed wall surface is only interrupted at a height of about 4 m by the small room window (g).

3. Façade, section E. In this part of the wall, also in opus incertum of lava, a walled arch is clearly recognisable. The opus incertum of the filling contains, in addition to lava, large limestone stones. The arch is also visible on the N wall of the room (k) behind. Probably in an earlier construction phase there was an opening here.

4. To the right and left of the entrance to the house, vertical and horizontal limestone orthostats make up the soffits. Until 1948 these were crowned by the figured capitals from which the house takes its name, currently preserved in the "Granary" of the Forum of Pompeii. DAIB 90.2.304 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

5. Entrance, O jamb, capital, external side: the N side of the western capital (inv. no. 298-4), 48.5 cm high, 77.4/"78 cm long, shows, among acanthus leaves and scrolls at the corners, the busts of a drunken Silenus and a Maenad. Both still retain traces of red color on the lips (Silenus also on the nipples) and dark in the pupils; on the beard of the Silenus traces of black and dark brown; in several points, especially on the corners, there are remains of a lime rinse.

6. Entrance, jamb O, capital, side of the vestibule (a): the face facing the vestibule shows a married couple half-reclining. The woman, on the left, seems to greet the observer with her raised hand, the male figure rests his right hand on his partner's shoulder. The man wears a crown, probably a corona tortilis, while the woman's head is covered by a veil or cloak. Here too there are remains of red on the lips of both and on the man's nipples and, in several places, traces of lime rinsing.

7. Entrance, jamb E, capital, external side: the capital to the E of the entrance (inv. no. 297-4) is more deteriorated. 47.8 cm high, with sides 80.7 and 77.5 cm long, it is very similar, in figurative and vegetal decoration, to capital O. On the outer face there are busts of a Silenus and a Maenad. Her hair is tousled by the lively movement of her head and her eyes wide open; he holds a torch that passes behind his head. Silenus, depicted three-quarters behind her, touches the woman's elbow with his right hand and rests his left on her shoulder. Considerably damaged by atmospheric agents, the relief has not preserved the chromatic layer, apart from traces of white lime.  DAIR 43.409

8. Entrance, jamb E, capital, side of the vestibule (a): here too we find the representation of a married couple. The relief is poorly preserved: of the woman, also in this case semi-lying on the left, only the outline of the head is visible. She is facing the man and rests her left hand on his shoulder. The man looks in the opposite direction, but in his left hand he holds the woman's right. As in capital O, the male figure has a braided circle. On the lips there are traces of red, only remains of the painted decoration, as well as the white lime behind the corner volutes. Both capitals, certainly dating back to the first construction phase, i.e. around 120 BC (cf. Staub Gierow 1994, p. 73), perhaps testify to the adherence of the inhabitants of the house to the cult of Dionysus, while the gesture of greeting of the woman depicted on capital O is probably to be interpreted as a variant of the mosaic emblem with the formula HAVE. The masonry is in the opus africanum widely used in this house, that is, in lava uncertain and limestone orthostats. The jambs of the opening of the fauces were once decorated with stucco half-pillars, the walls had frescoes in the "candelabra style", of which in the E section of the wall there are remains of white, ochre, light and dark red, blue and green. The floor covering is in papier-mâché with marble squares that form a diamond decoration.

A W of the tablinum, the room (q) leads into the peristyle (t) and into the room (r), on the W side of the house. The third door on the S side of the atrium leads to the oecus (s), located to the E. In front of the stretch of wall between the tablinum and the room (q), a richly decorated ark was found, of which only part of the base is currently preserved - a block of lava with an iron hook in the central part.

12. Ark, detail of the central relief plate.

On the S side is the travertine puteal (height 57 cm, upper diameter 48 cm, lower diameter 56 cm), cylindrical in shape and somewhat squat, with 32 grooves and short, slightly rounded tabs. Partridge dates the object to the post-Silla era (Pernice T, p. 29).

14. Atrium (b), wall O: the series of doors leading into rooms (h), (i) and (j) and wing (0), open in its full width onto the atrium. The short sections of wall between the gates are in opus africanum with opus incertum filling of lava.

Avellino (cited in the bibl.) describes them as "crudely painted, partly red and partly white". A stucco relief of the first or second style, noted by Mau, has also been lost; numerous nails and nail holes. The floor, very deteriorated, is in raw opus signinum. On the W wall is a coarse repair made with one of the later types of plaster attested in the house. DAIB 90.2.169 (Fot. P. Grunwald)

The back wall of this was restored in the later phase of renovation. 18. Room (i), wall N: here the last phase of restoration of the house, probably datable between 62 and 79 AD, is documented in a particularly significant way. Against the high N and S walls, which preserved in good condition remains of decoration in "candelabra style" from the early Augustan age, new walls were built that remained undecorated. At the time of the excavation, the primitive decoration of the O wall was also seen: tall and thin candelabra in the middle area and flowers in the frieze. The floor is in simple cocciopesto.
19. Room (i): detail of the oldest N wall (see fig. 18) with the remains of a fresco in which the calm colors of the "candelabra style" dominate, to which the painting must be attributed.

20. Room (j), wall N: it is the only room decorated in the IV style. The paintings have been preserved in a more satisfactory state on the N wall, even if only in pieces and up to the height at which the wall has been preserved, i.e. the upper part of the middle area. The plinth, 70 cm high, is red and divided by white lines into panels, three of which, wider, were decorated with tufts of leaves; in the remaining two were horse heads in profile painted in yellow. The middle area is divided into three fields separated by white pilasters (width 25.5 cm). The central and left fields are preserved in their entire width (1 m), the right only in fragments. In the fields, framed by a 5 cm wide perforated border, there were the figures described by Avellino as follows (cited in the bibl.): "a bacchante with thyrsus and a winged erote with basket". The side courts are red, the middle one yellow. The decoration probably dates back to the period between 62 and 79 AD.

21. Room (j), mosaic floor in black and white tiles. On a white background, two black-framed fields stand out. In the center of the narrower one, to the W, is a spiral of flower buds made of black tesserae, while the field of the front half (1.50 x 1.20 m) is undecorated. On the edges of the mosaic there are not only the wall decorations in the IV style, but also the remains of plaster pertaining to the previous decoration in the "candelabra style". Therefore, the spiral of bluebells, attributed by Pernice (Pernice, p. 145) to the II late style, certainly belongs to the decorations of the early Augustan age.

Peristilto (o), wall E of the N. portico The stylistic affinity with the paintings of the tablinum (1) and the oecus (m) is immediately evident from the drawings, characterized by the monochrome of the three areas into which the wall is divided: the plinth was black, as was the middle area, while the upper area had a red background; Similar to the scheme of the aforementioned rooms is also the central field of the middle area, configured as an aedicule framed by elegantly decorated columns. 52. Exedra (y), wall N. This wall, with a large opening on the peristyle and a window above, preserves small remains of the original decoration that has never been documented. The surviving passages, however, indicate that the decorative scheme must have been similar to that of the S wall, except for a few differences. The plinth, present only in the short sections of the wall aEe to the W of the opening, shows a yellow seahorse, where a lion griffin is depicted on the S wall. The narrow fields of the middle zone contain vegetable candelabra very similar to those of the lateral fields of the S wall. Even what remains of the decoration of the upper area reveals the same scheme as the S wall. Unfortunately, the central aedicule in which the seated figure that was a pendant with Zeus was probably represented is lost in this area.

53. Exedra (y), wall W, drawing by G. Abbate. In a good state of preservation at the time of discovery, the painting is now lost, with the exception of a few sections of the plinth, the edges of the middle area and some parts of the upper area. It can, however, be reconstructed thanks to the numerous reproductions available (Zahn II, fig. 53; Abbate, ADS 672; 671: cf. Disegnatori, pp. 238-239, figs. 1-2; Boulanger, Ecole Normale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts, Paris, vol. 11, 272; Hilker, Copenhagen Kunstakademie, inv. n.A11047a, A11047e, A11047f, A11047k). These show a marked resemblance to the S wall, both in the general scheme and in the details. The main difference lies in the subdivision into five fields instead of three as in the S wall, and in the fact that, even in the margins we find architecture. The plinth shows the same pattern, except for minor differences (rhombuses with lion heads instead of roundels with gorgonîon, swans in flight instead of the lion griffin). In the middle area, two architectural views, each containing a candelabrum, here of a simpler shape, flank the central field with a rectangular pinax. In the side fields are depicted groups in flight. A new element is also the slender architecture represented at the edges of the wall and which rise to the entire height of the middle area. Behind their half-open doors you can see golden statues of deities, on the left probably Dionysus crowned with thyrsus, on the right a deity no longer identifiable.

55. Esedra (y), W wall. The pinax of the central field of the middle zone, now disappeared, is known to us from two drawings preserved in Naples (ADS 673, 674: cf. Disegnatori, pp. 487, fig. 84; 211, fig. 99) and an illustration in Curtius (Curtius 1929, p. 397, fig. 216), as well as smaller reproductions as part of the overall representation of the wall. The composition is similar to that of the two pinakes on the S wall. In the background is a tree, in this case a myrtle, in front of which are placed a base with an ithyphallic statuette of Priapus and a rectangular altar. On the latter rest a thymiatérion and a tray. In front, on the right, a smaller altar is visible on which a diadem is placed. On the ground are represented a circular pyx, two doves, a horseradish and an amphora. The painting is enlivened by four small erotes, the one on the right, standing, holds a garland, the one on the left, seated, pulls a bracelet from a casket, while the two depicted in the background appear busy at the altar. The presence of all these elements leads us to relate the painting to the cult of Aphrodite. From a stylistic point of view, it must be considered together with that of the S wall, which refers to the cult of Ares. Mau (Mau W, pp. 2776 s.) had already noted the difference between these two paintings and the one with an allusion to Hera, hypothesizing that the former belonged to an older decoration in the second style of the exedra. The analysis of the plaster has shown the presence, under the last painted covering, of remains dating back to an earlier phase, pertaining to a decoration in the second style. ADS 674 (Fot. Pedicini)
